turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, I can break this down simply.

Think of it like choosing from a menu with just a few big decisions:

Pick what kind of plant
Roses: This is our main thing. Great if you want flowers all season for many years.
Perennials: Other long-lived plants (like lavender, catmint, daisies) that come back every year.
Bulbs: Things like tulips and daffodils that you plant (usually in fall) and they pop up in spring.
For roses, choose the “shape” of the plant
Climbing roses: Grow tall and need support (arch, fence, trellis). Good for walls and arches.
Shrub/bush roses: Rounded plants for beds and borders. Great general-purpose garden roses.
Groundcover/landscape roses: Low, spreading plants that cover an area.
Hybrid tea roses: Classic “long-stem” roses, usually one big bloom per stem, great for cutting.
Match your sun and climate
Sun:
Full sun = 6+ hours of direct sun. Most roses like this best.
Partial shade = about 4 hours of sun; choose "partial shade" or "shade tolerant" options.
Hardiness zone:
At the top of our website you can pick your zone (like Zone 6, Zone 8).
This filters to plants that can handle your winters.
Choose the fun stuff: color & fragrance
Color: You can filter for pink, red, white, yellow, orange, purple, etc.
Fragrance: You can choose lightly, moderately, or strongly fragrant roses depending on how much scent you want.
How our plants arrive
All roses: Own-root, in 1-gallon containers with soil. They arrive without leaves or buds at first, then leaf out and grow once planted.
Perennials: Also shipped in containers.
Bulbs: Packed dry in bags, planted directly in the soil at the right time.

If you’d like to read a bit more, our simple how-to pages are here: How-to articles.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question, and good thinking to start off on the right foot.

I’ll walk you through using the Get Growing Bundle the very first time. Do this the day you plant your rose.

SECTION 1: If you’re planting in the ground

Prepare the hole
Dig a hole about 2 feet wide and 2 feet deep.
Put about 3 inches of regular soil back in the bottom of the hole.
Add the amendments In a bucket or wheelbarrow, mix:
Some of your dug-out soil
A generous scoop of the cow manure
About 1 cup of bone meal
Some mint compost

Then:

Put some of this mixed soil back into the hole on top of that first 3 inches of plain soil.
Set the rose
Take the rose out of its container or compostable bag.
Place it in the hole so the old soil line is just slightly below your garden soil surface (about 1 inch deeper).
Fill around the roots with the rest of your soil + amendment mix.
Gently press the soil to remove big air pockets.
Water with fish fertilizer
Mix 4 oz of Founders Fish Fertilizer in 1 gallon of water (follow the label if you prefer).
Water the rose slowly at the base with this mixture.
After planting
Water normally (plain water) 2–3 times a week while it’s getting established.
You can use the fish fertilizer again every 4–6 weeks during the growing season.
Reapply mint compost as a light layer on top of the soil every 6 months.

SECTION 2: If you’re planting in a container

Make your potting mix In a tub or bucket, mix:
Your potting soil
Some cow manure
About 1 cup of bone meal
Plant the rose
Fill the container partway with this mix.
Set the rose in so the old soil line is just slightly below the top of the new soil.
Fill in around the roots with the mix.
Press gently to settle.
Top dress with mint compost
Spread a thin layer of mint compost on top of the soil around the base of the plant.
Refresh that top layer about every 6 months.
Water with fish fertilizer
Mix 4 oz of Founders Fish Fertilizer in 1 gallon of water.
Water the rose with this mix.
Repeat every 3–4 weeks during the growing season.
